paras: The Kirbyville triple lynching was the hanging of three unnamed men accused of leading a ring of horse thieves, carried out by vigilantes at a pinery near Kirbyville, Missouri, in mid-April 1882. Wire reports from Chicago and St. Louis carried the story nationally, describing it as the first triple hanging in that part of Missouri for several years. No report gave the race of the men killed.

According to St. Louis mail advices, a good deal of horse stealing had been done lately in the section around Kirbyville, in one of the southern counties of Missouri. The Chicago special said the people of the neighborhood had for some time been troubled by the depredations of horse thieves, and that three men were at length "discovered to be the ring leaders."

The three men were hunted down, taken to "the pinery, some distance from town," and hanged. The Chicago special said the deed was performed swiftly and the "vigilants" dispersed the moment the men were swung up, while the St. Louis advices attributed the hanging to "a party of citizens." The Ottawa Free Trader dated the hunt to 14 April, and the St. Louis version said only that it happened "a few days ago." The men's names were not known, but they were said to have come from Greene county, Missouri.

A Post-Dispatch special from Little Rock on 22 May placed the hanging within a longer chase, saying a band of vigilantes had pursued eight horse thieves for over two weeks. Of the five who escaped, it said, one had since been killed, one mortally wounded and one jailed, while two were hemmed in on White river and were expected to be captured and lynched. In early June the Hickman Courier reported that the gang infesting the border counties of Missouri and Arkansas had been broken up by local farmers, all but two lynched or imprisoned. No report of an inquest or of arrests of the vigilantes appears in the coverage.

The first word reached Chicago by telegram via Little Rock, and an early item in the Alexandria Gazette said there was "some doubt about the truth of the story." The same day, the Rock Island Argus and the Memphis Public Ledger printed fuller accounts, and the Wheeling Register ran the St. Louis advices with the Chicago special as "Another Account." On 16 April the Chicago special appeared in Seattle, Cheyenne, Los Angeles and St. Paul papers.

Headlines ranged from the plain "Triple Hanging" and "Horse Thieves Hanged" to the Memphis paper's "Horse Thieves Come to Grief" and the Cheyenne Daily Leader's "Is Missouri Civilized?" The reports called the dead "thieves" without qualification, and the Ottawa Free Trader grouped the case with an Alabama lynching under "Thriving Business of Judge Lynch." The May Little Rock wire ran in Maine, Montana and elsewhere, under headlines such as "Western Justice" and "The Work of Vigilantes." The only Missouri paper found, the Richmond Democrat, gave the story a single line.

The Richmond Democrat said eight horse thieves had been caught and lynched at Kirbyville, apparently merging the eight pursued with the three hanged in the other reports. A 23 May version of the Little Rock wire said the three were captured "a few days ago," which does not fit the April date given in earlier reports.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Chicago or St. Louis wire verbatim under headlines like 'Triple Hanging' and 'Horse Thieves Hanged', calling the dead 'thieves'.
The Cheyenne Daily Leader headed the wire 'Is Missouri Civilized?', while the Memphis Public Ledger used 'Horse Thieves Come to Grief'.
The Ottawa Free Trader placed it in a 'Thriving Business of Judge Lynch' roundup.

conflicts.note: The Ottawa date is the only explicit one; all agree on the days just before 15 April.
The Richmond Democrat brief appears to conflate the eight pursued with those lynched.
The doubt appears only in the first Chicago item; later reports repeat the hanging without qualification.
